newsitem.title: USA: Simpson begins testimony, denies hitting ex-wife.
newsitem.headline: Simpson begins testimony, denies hitting ex-wife.

text.p: Testifying in court for the first time since the 1994 murders of his ex-wife and her friend, O.J. Simpson repeatedly denied on Friday that he ever hit Nicole Brown Simpson but claimed that she struck him "numerous times."

Taking the witness stand in his civil trial, Simpson said his ex-wife physically attacked him in his Brentwood mansion one night in 1989 and that in defending himself he put her in a headlock and pushed her out of the bedroom.

"At that time, I was being wrongly physical with her," Simpson testified under sometimes harsh interrogation by the plaintiff's lead attorney, Daniel Petrocelli. "She jumped on me...and I reacted in a way I shouldn't have."

As jurors were shown photos of a bruised and battered Nicole Brown Simpson, the former football star said he could not remember inflicting the injuries. The incident, which took place in the early hours of New Year's Day, led to Simpson not contesting a charge of spousal abuse. Under California law, this is considered the same as a guilty plea.
Simpson testified on Friday that he and his ex-wife sometimes had heated arguments but he depicted himself as the victim of physical abuse at her hands.

Asked how many time she struck him during the course of their 17-year relationship, Simpson replied, "Numerous times." But he answered "never" when asked whether he ever hit, struck slapped, or choked Nicole Brown Simpson.

Simpson, 49, was acquitted of double-murder charges in October of last year, but he is now facing a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families, who are seeking to hold him responsible and financially "liable" for the killings.

Attorneys for the families have contended that Simpson physically abused, stalked and threatened his ex-wife, finally killing her in June 1994 when he could no longer control her. Her friend, Ronald Goldman, was stabbled to death beside her.

In his first confrontation with opposing attorneys, Simpson sat only a few feet (metres) from the jury box and answered questions mostly in a clear, confident voice. At times, however, he sighed deeply and his tone was nervous.

Simpson, 49, was acquitted of double-murder charges in October of last year, but he is now facing a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families, who are seeking to hold him responsible -- and financially "liable" -- for the killings.

While Simpson chose not to testify at his criminal trial, the rules of civil procedure required him to either take the witness stand or forfeit the case, which could have cost him millions of dollars in damages.
The courtroom was packed with Simpson's relatives and the victims' family members for what legal analysts say could be a crucial turning point in the two-month- old trial.
Attorneys for the families called Simpson to the stand as a hostile witness and want to destroy his credibility in the eyes of the jury by tripping him up in contraditions or inconsistencies.
The plaintiff's attorneys are expected to keep Simpson on the stand at least until next Tuesday, when the trial goes into Thanksgiving holiday recess until Dec. 2.

Friends say Simpson -- who enjoyed an all-American nice-guy image during his years as a star running back, sportscaster, advertising pitchman and actor -- has always had a knack for talking his way out of trouble.

But this may be the toughest test for Simpson. Opinion polls show Americans split along racial lines over the verdict in the criminal trial, with most whites saying Simpson got away with murder and most blacks believing in his innocence.

Simpson was cleared of murder charges by a mostly black jury, but the civil trial is being heard by a panel with a vastly different racial makeup -- nine whites, one black, one mixed Asian-West Indian and one person of mixed white and Hispanic descent.

Cameras are banned from the courtroom, but camera crews swarmed outside the courthouse, and a few demonstrators and publicity seekers turned out. But it was far more subdued than the frenzy that surrounded the first trial.
